Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Today I learned that my sister's Spanish class (middle school) is making each student change their name to a ‘Hispanic’ one if they have an “American” name (example Mark to Jose). Does anyone else find this alarming and very odd?
Answer: I went by “Manuel” in my middle school Spanish class 20 years ago, even though that’s not the equivalent of “Mark.” It was kind of a role-playing exercise, part of an attempt to immerse oneself in the culture of the language you were learning, and a lot of kids chose names that were different from their English ones. I understand that’s been standard practice in language instruction for a long time. Growing up, when someone was speaking to me in Polish they’d address me as “Marek”, and that’s how I preferred to be addressed when I lived in Poland. Consider that many Chinese or other Asian students coming to the US take on an “American” name that’s different from their given ones. Pop culture is full of examples of Americanizing names, hence viz. Israel Beilin becoming known as Irving Berlin, Ramon Estevez being known as Martin Sheen, or even Marion Morrison being known as John Wayne. Those who went to Catholic school may have an add-on saint’s name: my father-in-law went to Catholic school in Malaysia growing up, and was known as “Leon.” He hates it nowadays, but at the time, who knows. So no, it’s not odd or alarming.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why hasn’t Babe Ruth’s status as GOAT in baseball been deteriorated by time, like Pele in football (soccer)?
Answer: I think it has to do with the evolution of soccer and baseball. Soccer is a very different game today than it was in the 1960’s, with better equipment, fitter players, and different defensive and offensive schemes. Baseball, at least superficially, is the same game it has always been: you have a pitcher throwing to a batter 60 feet 6 inches away, and the batter trying to hit the ball with a stick. While there have been some changes that have favored the pitcher in that fundamental duel (Ruth probably never saw a slider, a split-fingered fastball, or a 100-mph fastball, for instance. He also wasn’t seeing statistically-informed defensive shifts, or relief pitching as we currently understand it today), there have also been some changes since Ruth’s time that have favored the batter (after his time the ball got livelier, the pitcher’s mound was lowered, and the seasons got longer). Basically, you could argue that the changes in his favor, and against him, would mostly cancel out, and Ruth would put up similar numbers today as he did in the 1920’s. It’s not as clear if Pele could do the same. This being said (and I’m surprised it doesn’t enter the debate), Major League Baseball in the 1920’s would not have the same caliber of players in it as it does today, for the simple reason that Black, Hispanic, and Asian players were not allowed in. There may well have been a Shohei Ohtani, or a CC Sabathia, or a Bob Gibson alive at that time, but Ruth would never have faced them because of the color barrier.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are any plays of the past 70 years, besides Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, worthy of placement alongside Oedipus the King, Hamlet, and King Lear?
Answer: I think the works of August Wilson are definitely up there, but for whatever reason he’s not as well known outside of Pittsburgh. A Raisin in the Sun is also extremely good. Steel Magnolias is a very good play, a better play than the movie adaptation. A Man for All Seasons is almost Neo-Shakespearian in the way that it is written, and in the subject matter that it talks about. It’s also an extremely good play. Arthur Miller writes extremely well, though some of his stuff can come off as over the top after a while. Noises Off is perhaps the funniest play I have ever seen. But you have to see it. On paper, it doesn’t look like much. Ultimately, however, it is impossible to know which plays are “as good”, or as enduring, as Sophocles, or Shakespeare, because not enough time has passed to allow lesser plays to be forgotten. It’s also hard to know which plays will stand the test of time once what they reference has passed from memory, because, well, we still remember what Arthur Miller was talking about. I can’t help but wonder if the entire genre of plays that could be titled “dysfunctional American families yelling at each other” will be quietly forgotten once the United States changes, disappears entirely, or no longer has the idea of the “American Dream” that, in its failure to be realized, hangs over most American plays of the 20th century.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Would a 'theoretical' metal heated at a temperature of 2000-8000° C be able to kill all* surface microbes (Assuming constant temperature)?
Answer: You don’t really need temperatures that high to kill everything or almost everything on a surface: if you run things through an autoclave at 15 psi of steam at 121C for an hour, that will pretty much take care of it. Dry-heat wise, you only need 160C for a few hours, and that will do the trick. Basically, you don’t need temperatures that high to ensure sterility, or a pretty good level of sterility.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What's the biggest no-no when you are a PhD student?
Answer: I like to talk about the dreaded “Three Nos” when giving a group meeting: no results, no plan, no clue. Generally, if you can answer “yes” to one of those (you have results, or a plan, or a clue), you will generally be OK. I’ve seen some very good presentations that go like this: “so, here was my hypothesis. After testing it 3 different ways, very rigorously, I can tell you that this system does not work this way, and we can’t build the thing I want to build. I’ll try this idea next.” If your adviser is sane, they will actually pat you on the back for this: that’s good science. Science frequently doesn’t work. OR, if your talk is “so, I’ve got these really weird results. I think they mean X, but I’m not sure. What do you guys think?” That’s also good: why do you have group meeting if not to share ideas? But what you don’t want to do is stand up there and say “yeah, I didn’t really do anything, and I’m not sure what I’m doing, and I don’t really know anything about anything,” because that shows a lack of effort and engagement. You’ve also letting yourself drift aimlessly, and that’s not the point of a PhD. I gave a related answer here:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does your PhD supervisor matter?
Answer: I would argue that your PhD supervisor is the most important factor in how your PhD goes. Consider: At the end of the day, you need to ask yourself, what matters to you? I feel like my PhD was sort of mediocre in terms of impact, and I’m not well-positioned for an academic career. Now, that happened in large part because of who I was as a student, and who I am as a person, but my advisor’s style contributed to it as well. On the other hand, my advisor’s style made it possible for me to enjoy graduate school. I had fun. I had hobbies, a life outside the lab, and that’s how I met my wife. I’ve seen a lot of people age 10–15 years during a 5-year program, leaving with a large number of gray hairs short of their 30th birthday. I know of at least one student who was starting to get health problems because of overwork. In my case maybe I got a little fatter, and while I had less hair at graduation than when I started, none of it was gray yet. I feel like I’m lucky: there are very few PhDs who can honestly say they miss graduate school, and I’m one of them. I ended up not caring about an academic career anyway, and the whole experience positioned me to make a good living doing something else. I think I learned the lessons I needed to learn to be successful in my chosen career. And I’m not really broken up about the fact that my PhD work didn’t get published in Science or Nature. So I think I got lucky when choosing an advisor. But that’s me. Other people in my shoes would see my PhD as a failure, or at least as a disappointment, and other advisors would probably have disowned me.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it surprising that so many Americans believe conspiracy theories? Why or why not?
Answer: It is not surprising, considering that Americans are humans. There are conspiracy theories all over the world, and they have existed throughout history. Basically, we’re not special, and I’ve heard all kinds of conspiracy theories from around the world (ask a certain type of Polish conservative about the Smolensk Disaster, for instance. Or ask someone in former Yugoslavia about damn near anything). Conspiracy theories are alive and well in Turkey. We tend to fixate on our own country, because it’s what we know. Why are there conspiracy theories? First, humans are experts at looking for explanations, reasons, and order where there might not be any. It’s why we see patterns in the sky, and invoke deities to explain the weather. So when something truly big happens, we assume there must be a big cause behind it, or alternately, we believe that complex events must have complex causes, when that’s not necessarily the truth (you can explain what causes an earthquake in about 5 minutes. The effects of an earthquake, however, are long-lasting). Further, belief in a conspiracy theory is oddly comforting, because it gives the illusion that someone is in control. Belief in a conspiracy theory also makes someone feel smart: they have hidden knowledge that all the “sheeple” don’t. It makes them feel important: they think they are exposing a hidden truth, rather than just ranting on the internet. There is a community aspect of this as well: we, the smart people, are enlightened, unlike they, the dumb, manipulated people. What might explain conspiracy theories specifically in America? Question: I’m a 67-year-old cashier. My coworker is 19 and tries talking to me like an equal. How do I put him in his place and remind him that as an elder, I deserve unconditional respect and obedience?
Answer: You know, I’ve noticed that some people manage to become old without becoming wise. I think you are one of those people. “Unconditional respect and obedience”: if an 80 year old told you to go jump in a lake, you’d better do it and thank him for telling you to do so, by that logic.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is "Richard II" by William Shakespeare worth the read?
Answer: Other commentators on Quora point out, rightly I think, that Shakespeare is meant to be seen. So it’s probably best to see the play first, done by a good ensemble, then read it. I recommend the BBC’s “Hollow Crown”, starring Ben Whishaw in the title role, Rory Kinnear as Bolingbroke, Patrick Stewart as John of Gaunt, and David Suchet as the Duke of York. There’s also a hilarious Shakespeare webcomic called Good Tickle Brain that presents Richard II in stick figures. It’s an accurate summary, and I love this site for all things Shakespeare: That being said, yes, Richard II is absolutely worth the read. It is an often-overlooked, and in my opinion very underrated play. The central question faced by the protagonists is, what do you do when you have a legitimate ruler who sucks, and there’s a challenge to him from some guy who is a better ruler, but his claim to power sucks? Richard II isn’t exactly a tyrant, he’s just bad at his job and strongly implied to be gay. Does that mean you can get rid of him? And if you do get rid of him, where’s the line between doing what you’re doing because you care about your country, and doing it because you are an opportunist? These are some serious philosophical questions which are carried through to the other plays of the “Henriad”, namely 1 Henry IV, 2 Henry IV, and Henry V. 1 Henry IV is just about my favorite Shakespeare play, I think you can skip 2 Henry IV, and Henry V is pretty good. But back to Richard II: The language is magnificent. It’s some really, really good writing, and it also differentiates its characters very well: Richard is dramatic, Bolingbroke is very businesslike. Now, I’d say this shouldn’t be the very first Shakespeare play you read, because the language is very stylized and almost all of the play is in verse. But if you’re already familiar with how Shakespeare writes, then this is well worth the read. I mean, just look at this! For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed; Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd; All murder'd: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp, Allowing him a breath, a little scene, To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks, Infusing him with self and vain conceit, As if this flesh which walls about our life, Were brass impregnable, and humour'd thus Comes at the last and with a little pin Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king! Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood With solemn reverence: throw away respect, Tradition, form and ceremonious duty, For you have but mistook me all this while: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should I base my decision on when choosing a research group for my MSc thesis and future PhD (Chemistry)? Should I worry about the size of the group and the PI’s way of supervising?
Answer: I would advise you to base your decision more on personality of the group and less on what the group is actually doing. Part of that is me: I’ve been able to find the interesting parts of some very different fields of research, and others might have trouble making that adjustment, but my advice is find a pleasant group, and then find a way to make your work interesting within that group. The number one mistake you can make is to think that you’re special. It’s easy to think “oh, this professor is a jerk, but they’ll be nice to me” or “this group takes a long time to graduate, but I’ll make it out in five years because I’m me.” No. The problems of a group will apply to you as well. What do I mean on personality of the group? Well, 1) what are the expectations of work hours/work-life balance? And do you find such a schedule agreeable? If the boss has a reputation for insisting his group work 80-hour weeks, and you don’t want to, that’s setting the stage for unhappiness. 2) How hands-on is the professor? By that I mean, is he telling you what to do constantly, or do you never see him? There are some groups where the professor is in lab every day. There are other groups where you don’t see the professor for months at a time. There are advantages and disadvantages to each management style: some people need more guidance, some people find guidance annoying. Ask yourself, how closely do I want to be managed? 3) Does the professor play favorites? Does the professor pit his students against one another, working on the same project to see who “wins”, and is that healthy or toxic competition? 4) Do the people in the research group seem to like each other, or are they constantly at each other’s throats? 5) How long does it take to graduate, and why? Also have to ask yourself about what’s important to you: do you want to graduate in 4.5 years after working 80+ hour weeks, or do you want to graduate in 7 years after working 40–50 hour weeks? Be wary of groups where there’s only one grad student left, and he’s been there for 8 years. Those are the biggest things, I think.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What does it mean when a referee holds up a yellow card?
Answer: In soccer, this is known as a “caution.” It means that a player or coach has been formally warned for a semi-serious offense. I write down the player’s number, the time of the infraction, and the reason. If the same player or coach commits another yellow card offense in the same game, they get kicked out (red card, or “sending-off”). Unlike in many other sports, being sent off means your team is playing short-handed….for the rest of the game. So, if you get a red card in the 5th minute, your team is playing with 10 men against the other teams’ 11 for the next 85 minutes. For hockey fans, that’s a permanent power-play. What are the reasons for getting a yellow card? Here they are: Of course, discretion applies. If I think a player really didn’t hear the whistle stopping play, and cleared the ball, I’m not going to caution for delaying restart of play. In youth games I rarely caution for failure to respect the distance, I’ll just tell the kid to back off and he usually does. On the other end of the spectrum, when do you give a yellow as opposed to a red, which is an ejection? Well, red is for violent conduct or serious foul play. What’s the line between “reckless” and “serious foul play?” Up to the referee. Or, is it stopping a promising attack (yellow), or is it denial of a goal-scoring opportunity (red)? Every situation is different, and that’s why you have a referee. There’s a whole little ceremony that’s supposed to accompany a yellow card. The referee is supposed to modulate his or her whistle to match the severity of the foul: a small foul, I’ll give a quick “chirp” on the whistle. But if something’s serious, it should be a long “TWEEEEET!” Ideally, the players should know from the whistle that a card is coming out. Then, giving the card itself: First, the referee should run over to where the foul is, then separate and isolate the player being cautioned/carded, so everybody knows who it is. I’ll usually go “red #17, step this way please” while taking the card out. Then, the referee holds the card over his or her head, then the referee writes down the player’s information. I usually talk to the player as well, saying something like “red #17, you are cautioned for a reckless challenge” before holding up the card. If it is a SECOND yellow card, the referee first holds up the yellow card, then holds up the red card, then points to the bench with a dramatic flourish, then writes everything down. The player has been sent off. The rules of competition sometimes also specify that the player who gets the yellow card has to go sit on the bench. They can be replaced on the field, and come back on at the next opportunity to substitute. That’s called a “hot-head” rule, and not all leagues have it: high school has it, a lot of recreational leagues have it, USSF and FIFA do not. You can be carded twice on the same play, and thrown out! This is usually funny to watch on YouTube: usually a player commits a reckless tackle at one end of the field. The referee signals “advantage”, meaning that he saw the foul but is letting play continue because it is to the advantage of the team that was fouled. That doesn’t erase the yellow card, however! The referee makes a mental note to issue the card at the next stoppage of play. So, play continues, and the fouling player runs down the field, and takes the guy with the ball out (stopping a promising attack). The referee will pull out the yellow, point to the spot of the first foul, show the yellow, then point to the spot of the second foul, then show the yellow followed by the red.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should this war be called, Ukraine/Russia war or Russia/America proxy war in Ukraine?
Answer: How about the War of Ukrainian Independence. That’s what it’s all about, isn’t it? If Russia wins, Ukraine will no longer be independent (and that was the Russian intent in the first place). If Ukraine wins, it will remain independent and choose whom to align with. It’s somewhat obnoxious how some commentators talk about Ukraine as though it doesn’t exist: they talk as though there’s Russia, then there’s Europe west of the Oder River, and all those guys in between the Oder and the Donets don’t really matter and can be disposed of as we please. But there *are* people there, who are as deserving of their own political independence as any others. So, War of Ukrainian Independence. That’s my vote.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why does it matter if bacteria is gram-positive or gram-negative?
Answer: Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria respond to different antibiotics, meaning that determining gram-positivity or gram-negativity of the bacteria in an infection lets you know the best course of treatment. Historically, finding out whether a bacterium was gram-positive or gram-negative was an important part of determining what kind of bacterium you actually had, along with what its shape was, how fast it grew, what kinds of medium it could grow on, etc. Nowadays we can do this pretty quickly and easily by DNA sequencing, but that’s only been a plausible option for the last 10–15 years. And in practice in a medical setting, it still might be cheaper to identify bacteria this way (I work in a research lab setting, so I don’t know what current best-practice is in hospitals). From a synthetic biology perspective, if you’re looking to do genetic engineering on a bacterium, the difference between gram-positive and gram-negative is very important. The thick outer peptidoglycan layer of a gram-positive bacterium makes it difficult to insert DNA into the cell, and you usually have to add enzymes or something to shave off some of that peptidoglycan. Gram-negative bacteria, on the other hand, are usually easier to get a plasmid into, and one of the many nice things about E. coli as a synthetic biology workhorse is that it is gram-negative, and easy to transform.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why have so many Americans fallen for conspiracy theories about Covid-19 being made in a lab?
Answer: I think an important distinction needs to be made. There are TWO theories out there, only the first of which you could call a conspiracy theory: That said, the reasons people believe COVID conspiracy theories is the same as the reasons they believe in any conspiracy theory. First, humans are experts at looking for explanations, reasons, and order where there might not be any. It’s why we see patterns in the sky, and invoke deities to explain the weather. So when something truly big happens, we assume there must be a big cause behind it, or alternately, we believe that complex events must have complex causes, when that’s not necessarily the truth (you can explain what causes an earthquake in about 5 minutes. The effects of an earthquake, however, are long-lasting). Further, belief in a conspiracy theory is oddly comforting, because it gives the illusion that someone is in control. Belief in a conspiracy theory also makes someone feel smart: they have hidden knowledge that all the “sheeple” don’t. It makes them feel important: they think they are exposing a hidden truth, rather than just ranting on the internet. There is a community aspect of this as well: we, the smart people, are enlightened, unlike they, the dumb, manipulated people. Or maybe people don’t actually believe in conspiracy theories. They just want you to think people believe in conspiracy theories.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do parents think they know what's best for their kids when they actually barely know us at all most the time? I'm just wondering because my parents always say like, "Oh, because I know what's best for you!" Or something along those lines.
Answer: I’m in my 30s, so I think I’ve got a little of your parent’s perspective, but also remember what it was like to be young, so please hear me out. There are two downsides to having life experience. The first is that you tend to downplay the crises of early adulthood, and the second is, you forget what it was like to not have that experience. Some of the things that were a huge deal for me back in high school (where will I go to college? Does Hannah like me? Does anybody like me?), really don’t matter now: I went to a college that was good-enough, I found a woman who was a better fit for me than Hannah was, and I moved out of state and haven’t been in touch with anyone from High School in years, so now none of that popularity stuff really matters. So it’s easy for me to say “ah, that was just kid’s stuff, I didn’t really have to worry.” But that’s only because I know more of my life’s story. At the time, it was a huge deal, my feelings about them were real, and I didn’t know that everything was going to turn out alright. To put this in perspective, what was something you were really upset about, or really worried about, when you were six years old? Does any of that stuff bother you now? Believe it or not, when you get older, you’ll feel the same about the age you are right now. The other problem, forgetting what it was like to not have that experience, means that it’s hard to logically explain to someone why a certain course of action is a bad idea, because, well, it’s perfectly obvious to you. Think about a baby crawling to the edge of a table or cliff. Can you explain to the baby, rationally and in a way that they will understand, why it’s a bad idea to crawl closer to that edge? Similarly, there are some “cliffs of life” that seem so damn *obvious* after you’ve lived for a while, that it’s hard to explain what they are exactly, or why they are dangerous. You can quote statistics or something, but it’s hard to convince someone using those statistics, because (and adults make this mistake too!), we are all convinced that we will be one of the lucky ones who beats the odds. A challenge for parents is, not all cliffs are equally dangerous. I think about all the mistakes I made, and all the pain I felt as a result, and I want my kid to avoid making the same mistake, and feeling the same pain. I also think about all the mistakes I’m really glad I *didn’t* make, which I know that some of my classmates did make (alcohol, drugs, pregnancy, reckless driving), and I really, really don’t want my kid to fall down that path, because I’ve seen what happens. If I thought my kid were going down that bad path, I would no doubt make myself extremely obnoxious in trying to change their course. But there are two problems here. The first is, some of those very painful mistakes taught me some very valuable lessons, things I would not have learned otherwise. And even if I could go back in time and say “hey, I’m you, from the future. Don’t do X”, I know I wouldn’t have listened. On the other hand, if I had gone back in time and said “be sure not to drink and drive!”, past-me would have said “thank you, Captain Obvious!” Last, you have to remember that your parents grew up in a different world, with different problems and ways of solving them. If you were suddenly transported back to 1990, how do you order a pizza? Find your way to a party? Figure out where the party was happening? Remember, no smartphones or even cell phones unless you were really rich! Bottom line is, your parents would know how to do this, and they might still largely do it this way because it still works. They didn’t have to contend with social media or some of the other dreadful things of our modern era, and so don’t really know how to deal with them exactly. And a funny thing about the internet: I remember, back in the early-to-mid 90’s, that the internet was considered a reputable source of information. It’s true! It used to be a nerdy, academic thing, with most of the content being created and curated by the kinds of people who knew how to code while also having an interest in beekeeping. Boy howdy, are things different now. However….. What your parents are going off of is analogous (perhaps “analogue-ous”) experience. And while it might not be perfectly fitting to what you are experiencing today, it might still be valuable because people, and institutions, by and large, have not changed. The cyberbullies of today are basically the same insecure losers as the face-to-face bullies of yesteryear. Rumors that circulate on Facebook today would have circulated in the hallways at school back in 2001. I’d hear urban legends in the school cafeteria, before it was called “fake news.” The school administration was constantly coming up with stupid “school spirit” events in my day too. I had girls I was interested in not answering my phone messages. So maybe instead of focusing on the letter of your parents’ advice, focus on the spirit of it. Odds are, they know more than you might think.

Question: Why did General Robert E. Lee ultimately decide to lay down his arms after learning about the events of Appomattox?
Answer: How bad was the situation for the Confederates at Appomattox? It was so bad, Phillip Sheridan was actually kind of disappointed that Lee surrendered, because Sheridan was rather looking forward to conducting a massacre. After he was ordered not to attack, because the Confederates had come into Union lines with a white flag, Sheridan was seen stamping around, saying “we’ve got ’em like THAT!” and striking his hand with his fist. “Smash ’em up! Smash ’em up!” was one of his favorite things to say.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If the U.S. became independent in 1676, 1876, or 1976 instead of 1776, how prominently would the prevailing ideologies of the day have influenced the new nation's constitution as compared with the one that was adopted in 1789?
Answer: 1676: you probably would have ended up with a loose federation, or even 10–12 separate countries rather than a single united polity. It’s also important to note that Georgia hadn’t been founded yet, and the colonies in general were still very sparsely populated. What probably would have happened, historically, is that without British backing and military support, the French would have eventually swallowed the new United States. But in terms of ideology, 1676 was right when we were seeing the first glimmerings of the Enlightenment. The Glorious Revolution hadn’t happened yet. You would have probably seen a more religious Constitution, which may or may not have had a Bill of Rights. There probably would have been a monarch, either elected or otherwise. And it is possible that there would not have been a written constitution, because written constitutions only became fashionable after 1787 (the US Constitution is the oldest explicit and written constitution!) 1876: It depends on the scenario that creates a United States in this year. If we were still a British colony, independence probably would have looked something like the independence of Canada or Australia: a slow loosening of control on Britain’s part, and the formation of a federal Dominion, still nominally under the rule of the Queen, but for the most part self-governing under a copy of the Westminster System. The US probably would be a Parliamentary democracy, under a constitution similar to Canada’s. It would be the US of Eh. Canada was organized as a Confederation in 1867, and did not become fully independent until 1931, though the Queen is still officially the Head of State. Slavery would have been outlawed in 1833, along with the rest of the British Empire. That might have triggered a failed War of Independence along the lines of the American Civil War, but on the other hand, Britain didn’t really have a serious problem enforcing anti-slavery legislation…..with the exception of South Africa, where the Boers decided to move inland with their slaves in the Great Trek, and found two independent republics (Transvaal and the Orange Free State). These were a thorn in the side of Britain, but were eventually annexed into the Union of South Africa in 1902. Might something similar have happened in the US, with slave-owners pushing West and establishing separate countries that would eventually be annexed? It’s an interesting question. Now let’s say the scenario is different, and the US had developed as a set of separate states in loose confederation. Well, this was a time of nationalism and unification in Europe, with modern Germany being founded in 1871 and modern Italy being founded around the same time. You might have seen a similar process in the US, with the individual states recognizing that they had a lot in common. The country probably would have organized along German lines, as a federal parliamentary republic. 1976: The Constitution would have been very, very long, like the EU constitution. More recently written constitutions have attempted to deal with a whole bunch of things, from human rights to trade rights to name-of-origin rules to taxation…..they tend to be very cumbersome documents, rather than a rough sketch that is filled in later with legislation.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the general reaction of professors when students confront them about grades or assignments?
Answer: My general reaction is to groan when a student asks me about a grade. Now, if I made a mistake (either I have the wrong answer in the answer key, or I penalized something incorrectly), please let me know, that does happen, and I’m happy to correct myself. I’m not perfect. I’m also fine when someone comes to me early in the semester and says “I need help, what do I need to do?” If someone is having problems at home that make it difficult for them to get things done, and they make me aware of it early, then I’m sympathetic. However, it is more usual for someone to come to me at the end of the semester with a bunch of excuses, or to say in essence, “sure I didn’t do the work, and I won’t do it now, but will you raise my grade anyway?” Uh, no. Because it’s not fair to your classmates: I don’t know what struggles or sacrifices they had to make to get the grades they did. But if I allow people to sweet-talk me into higher grades, it means if you worked for your grade, you’re a sucker. I’m not going to do that.

Question: The “big three” of the classical world is always considered to be Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven. Apart from these, who would your big three be?
Answer: It’s really hard to limit it to just three, because there are a lot of great composers out there, and even more pretty good composers who had great moments. Haydn definitely has to be up there. I think his reputation has suffered from the fact that in addition to his masterpieces, he also wrote a lot of crap: he was writing on command, and a lot of his pieces came about because someone went “oh, court composer, the Prince wants something new to amuse his guests next Thursday. You can do that, can’t you?” But when he was writing to make an impact (like in his Esterhazy Masses, and his late oratorios The Creation and The Seasons), wow. He was also very inventive, could be funny, wrote for a wide range of instruments and forces, and his style evolved over time. Brahms would also be up there, for his technical proficiency if nothing else. He has the reputation for being boring, but that’s a performance challenge. To play Brahms properly, an ensemble has to be very good with phrasing and dynamics, because Brahms has the unusual property of requiring very precise phrasing. And that is really advanced, and perhaps underappreciated, music-making. Stravinsky, I think, also rates a mention for the influence he had on how music developed in the 20th century. From the choral perspective, Claudio Monteverdi, Giovanni da Palestrina, Thomas Tallis, William Byrd, Tomas Luis de Victoria all rate mentions, because I feel like they are kind of obscure outside of choral circles. But they are all great. Monteverdi did things in the 17th century that wouldn’t be done again until the mid-20th century.

Question: Is it fair to end a conversation with a scientist if he or she says that oxygen is really a kind of poison?
Answer: It is essential to human life, but despite that, oxygen IS a kind of poison: it will kill certain bacteria known as obligate anaerobic bacteria, for instance. Respiration, which uses oxygen and is what keeps our cells going, also leads to the formation of radical species that cause cellular damage. This damage is quickly repaired by cells, and cells are gradually replaced throughout our lives, but eventually as we age, our bodies become less able to repair the damage caused by the processes that keep us alive. In short, we are all slowly rusting. High concentrations of oxygen can be dangerous: when breathing oxygen at high partial pressures, you can get unpleasant effects on the lungs and nervous systems, like convulsions, dizziness, even seizures: Oxygen toxicity - Wikipedia This is also not to mention the fact that high oxygen concentrations will lead to very intense fires, as we saw on Apollo 1: Apollo 1 - Wikipedia Chemists using liquid nitrogen are warned about the dangers posed by liquid oxygen. In some cases when you’re using a vacuum line, you cool part of that vacuum line with liquid nitrogen. It’s called a cold trap, and it lets you get a much higher vacuum. However, we are repeatedly warned to pump the vacuum down to a pretty low level before we apply the liquid nitrogen, and this is because if you apply the liquid nitrogen right away, at atmospheric pressure, you will create liquid oxygen in the trap. It’s a beautiful blue color, but if you see it, you’re supposed to stop what you’re doing, turn off the vacuum, ventilate, and whatever you do, don’t do any chemistry while ventilating. The reason for that is, oxygen reacts with damn near everything. Concentrated oxygen reacts very quickly with damn near everything. There is a risk of explosion if you see liquid oxygen in your cold trap. In conclusion, just because something is vital to life doesn’t mean it isn’t also a poison. That goes for a lot of things that are vital to life: a little phosphorous is essential, but too much phosphorous is deadly, in very nasty ways. You need a tiny amount of selenium, but more than that, and you’re in trouble. As the old adage goes, ’tis the dose that makes the poison.

Question: How do antibiotics create resistant bacteria?
Answer: It isn’t so much that antibiotics *create* resistant bacteria, as that they *select* for resistant bacteria/give bacteria that are already resistant an evolutionary advantage. Bacteria (and everything else, really) are constantly mutating. Most of these mutations don’t do anything at all, some of these mutations are bad, and a very small number of them are beneficial to the bacterium in some way, but usually only in a very specific situation. For example, let’s say a bacterium has a mutation that allows it to survive in the antibiotic chloramphenicol. If there isn’t any chloramphenicol in the environment, this bacterium is not going to survive any longer, or replicate any faster, than its neighbors who don’t have the mutation. The gene exists, but who cares? It’s present in only a small subset of the population. However, when chloramphenicol is present, then suddenly all of the bacteria in the population are dead, *except* the population that has the resistance gene. And now it is surviving longer, and replicating faster, than cells that don’t have the gene, and after a while your population is made up of bacteria that have chloramphenicol resistance. Now, in real life, this would probably proceed incrementally: lets say you have a mutation that allows a bacterium to survive in chloramphenicol…..kind of. Instead of doubling every 20 minutes, the cells double in 2 hours. That’s still a huge advantage over cells that either straight-up die, or double in 4 hours. OK, so you have this population that doubles in 2 hours. Remember, those cells are still mutating! So the cell that is lucky enough to mutate so that it can now double every 90 minutes….has an advantage over the cells that still double in 2 hours. As long as the chloramphenicol is still present, cells that are better at defeating the chloramphenicol have an evolutionary advantage. As I like to say, “evolution is not your friend.”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Would a professor be upset if a student missed his office hours?
Answer: Uhh….no. Most of the time during my office hours, nobody would show up and I’d be grading or playing Solitaire or something. The default condition was, nobody came to my office hours. And as far as I’m concerned, if you’re a college student, you’re an adult, and if you don’t want to use the resources available to you, that’s your choice. Now, where I *would* get upset is when a student would be struggling, wouldn’t come to office hours, and would complain at the end of the semester that they got a bad grade. I’m sorry, but I was available to you, you didn’t take advantage of it, and what do you want me to do about it right now? You made a choice. On the other side of the coin, I’ve had students who have been on the bubble grade-wise, who *did* come to office hours all the time, and were clearly putting in a lot of effort. When I see a student like that, I’m inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt and give them, say, a solid B rather than a B-minus.

Question: Why are there so many racial issues in the United States? Are there similar issues in similar countries?
Answer: As I see it, the original sin of the United States was being a country founded on the equality of all men…..while at the same time relying on slave labor for a lot of the economy. Add to that the fact that slavery was racially-based. Now, other countries have had slavery (and it still happens!), but the US was founded on an idea that everybody was born free. Now, when people pointed this out to some of the Founding Fathers, their reaction was to look at their shoes, mutter something about “well, we kinda don’t like it either, and it’s bad, but slavery will die out. Eventually. We hope.” then quickly change the subject. Of course, this is not a great answer if somebody doesn’t let you change the subject. Furthermore, slavery may have been dying a natural death in 1790, but with westward expansion and new technologies like the cotton gin, slavery became *more* important to the economy in the 1820s. And it was at this point that guys like John C. Calhoun started making positive defenses of slavery, even making oxymoronic statements like “our liberty depends on the institution of slavery.” So, how do you justify promoting both human equality, and promoting slavery? Well, you have to see the slaves as subhuman. Confederate Vice-President Alexander Stephens put it very bluntly in his “Cornerstone” speech, that as he saw it, the error of the founding of the United States was that all men are created equal. He argues that this is false: Alexander Stephens on Slavery and the Confederate Constitution, 1861 Late in the Civil War, when the Confederacy was clearly losing, some Confederates said that the Army should enlist slaves as fighting men, with the promise of freedom if they somehow turned the tide. Even at that late date, with defeat staring him in the face, Stephens said if we allow slaves to enlist, we are saying that they are the equals of white men. And if they are the equals of white men, then the entire system of slavery, around which the Confederacy is based, is wrong. While they were promoting the idea that Black people are inherently inferior/subhuman, the Southern aristocracy had another problem: why would poor Southern whites, who couldn’t afford slaves, support slavery? Economically, slavery was bad for poor whites: if you are a farmer, how can you possibly compete in the marketplace with an enormous plantation that doesn’t have to pay people? If you’re looking to work for wages as a farmer on somebody else’s land, you’re out of luck, because you can’t compete with unpaid labor. If you want to move west…..oops, all the best land has already been taken by planters. Want to change things in the state legislature? Well good luck, because the people there are….planters. Why would you support this system? Well, because slavery has given you, a peasant, basically, a status you wouldn’t otherwise have: you may be poor and starving, but at least you’re white and that gives you someone to feel superior to. And those old habits die hard. Now, other ethnic groups were disliked when they first came to America. While “no Irish need apply” appears to be a myth, there was definitely anti-Irish sentiment, or anti-Catholic sentiment that was basically anti-Irish sentiment. Was there antisemitism in this country? You bet, and it has been making an unfortunate return. Italians and Poles were viewed with suspicion, and in 1900, they would not have been seen as “white.” Even as late as the 1950’s, my dad remembers being taunted with “hey you little Communist, go back to Russia where you belong.” I bring this up not to say “oh, poor white people”, but rather, to point out that there were once groups that were disliked, for racial reasons, who are now just lumped in that category of “generic white people.” I think we need to ask ourselves the question, how were we able to integrate these foreign ethnic groups, yet Blacks were still left out in the cold, as a race and people somehow apart? All that being said, I feel like in the US we often act as though our country invented racism, or that racism is a uniquely American problem. It is not. My father-in-law is ethnically Chinese, but grew up in Malaysia in the 1960s, where there is a sizeable Chinese minority. He remembers not being able to go to the beach, because that was “Malay territory”, and if you were on the beach while Chinese, you’d get beaten up. There were race riots in Malaysia at that time, which he doesn’t talk about. Even today, under the guise of “affirmative action”, there is legal discrimination against the Chinese minority by the Malay majority government, such as quotas for university admissions and government jobs. Apartheid South Africa was not a fun place to be if you were anything other than white. From what I know about Apartheid, it sounds like Jim Crow on steroids, and it is frankly amazing (and a testament to the leadership skills of Nelson Mandela, among others) that there was a peaceful transition to majority rule. Racism exists in places where, to our eyes at least, everybody looks the same. Former Yugoslavia is a great example of this: most Americans, I would venture, would have a hard time telling a Serb from a Croatian from a Bosnian from a Kosovar. On top of that, they speak pretty much the same language. Yet they spent the better part of 5 years killing each other over differences in religion, and there was genocide committed against the Bosniaks. This was less than 30 years ago. The Nigerian Civil War (Biafran War) had a distinct racial component, pitting the Igbo ethnic group against the Yoruba and Hausa-Fulani ethnic groups. The war started after a series of race riots: Rwanda in 1994 was another example of genocide brought about by racism. It’s also sometimes hard to separate the difference between racism and tribalism. My friend Robert was a Ugandan who was born in Sudan. He pointed out that he looked a bit like Idi Amin, and there was a reason for that: they both came from the same tribe. When Amin was deposed, there was a backlash against the members of his tribe, so Robert’s parents got the hell out of Uganda and ended up in a refugee camp, where Robert was born. The sanitary conditions in the camp were not good, so Robert contracted hepatitis as a child, and had chronic hepatitis his entire life, which eventually killed him about 30 years later.

Question: Is it possible for us to invent like a bag that contains predigested food and when we need large amounts of energy we hook the bag to our blood stream and therefore we get rapid amounts of energy instantly?
Answer: Interestingly enough, one hypothesis for why obesity has become so prevalent in the developed world is that we tend to eat a lot of processed foods. The processing makes the food softer, and easier to digest, meaning that we get more net calories from the processed foods (which are in a sense, pre-digested), rather than an equivalent amount of food that isn’t as processed (and which we have to invest more energy in actually breaking up).

Question: Is there an opposite to the Eureka moment?
Answer: Oh yes, those happen frequently in the sciences. Sometimes things will fail,and fail pretty spectacularly. You can have “oh crap!” moments, when something breaks. OR, you can have a Eureka moment, and you think you are really on to something…..then you recalculate and find out you were wrong. Or you have a Eureka moment, but then you do another control experiment and…..nope, it wasn’t as exciting as you thought it was. The moral of the story is, always do the right control experiments, and don’t get too discouraged when things don’t work out.

Question: If a book is resting on a table, Earth exerts a force on the book and the book exerts an equal force on Earth. Is this a Newton's third law pair?
Answer: Yes, it is a Third Law pair. Believe it or not, the Earth is getting pulled up just a tiny amount by the book resting on the table! Another third-law pair in this situation would be the force that the book exerts on the table, and the force that the table exerts on the book (the “Normal Force”).

Question: I had a “date” [we went to the rollercade] with this guy today who goes to my school but it didn’t feel right. He told me he had fun and when I think about it, I feel off. Why do I feel like this?
Answer: You might never know why you feel off about someone, but trust your gut. You are under no obligation to date anybody, and you don’t need a reason to not date them. If something seems wrong, don’t talk yourself out of that feeling, or rationalize it. Just trust it, and move on. On the flip side, when I started dating my wife, it felt right, and I couldn’t tell you exactly why. It still feels right 7 years later. If you are looking for a long-term partner, I would recommend prioritizing feeling comfortable, and feeling right, as opposed to feeling passionate.

Question: My significant other texted me that she no longer wants to talk to me. What should I say after reading her text?

I had exactly this sort of thing happen to me, and I saved a lot of time and anguish by respecting her request, and never talking to her again. It really hurts now, I know, but in a few years, when you have moved on, it will just be one of those things.
